title: Companies and foundations named in the waiver papers, and what the City pays them
question: Which organizations do the waiver requests, presentations and reports name as interested parties, partners or donors, and how much has the City paid them?
finding: The papers name 70 organizations (and 2 private individuals, counted, not named); 32 of them are City payees under the same or a similar name. The homelessness department's November 2025 memo lists the San Francisco Housing Accelerator Fund among interested parties engaged under the previous waiver and says any entity contracting with it is one; the City has paid that fund $55.9 million since fiscal 2019 (MYR $54.5 million, HOM $1.0 million, DEM $337,996). Its October 2024 request says of the philanthropies then named that "none of the partners above are contractors with the department", while its March 2024 slide lists among partnership names Larkin Street Youth Services (the soliciting offices' departments, HOM, MYR, paid it $119.6 million together) and Urban Alchemy (the soliciting offices' departments, HOM, MYR, paid it $72.5 million together). Of the Civic Bridge partner companies (waiver payor class "Various City contractors"), the largest City payees, leaving aside the employees' health plan (Blue Shield) and the University of California, are AECOM $216.9 million; AT&T $47.1 million; Deloitte $26.9 million; California State University–San Francisco $6.9 million; Accenture $5.9 million.
how: Names are taken from the bullet lists in the request memos and presentations, the Civic Bridge partner lists, the waiver reports, the India Basin resolution and draft funds agreement attached to the files. Each is matched to City payee names with a written pattern and payments are summed from fiscal 2019. "Paid by the soliciting office" counts only the departments of the officials who sought the waiver (for example HOM for the homelessness department).
limits: Name matches: a parent and its subsidiaries can carry different payee names, and payments to a university or health plan (Regents of the University of California, Blue Shield) are mostly for services unrelated to the waiver. Being named in waiver papers means an office talked to, or listed as a possible partner, the organization; it does not mean the organization was asked for money, gave, or received anything in return. Civic Bridge partners give staff time, not cash.
